description: People mapping (Phase 4a, settled by Ben 2026-10-28). One row per source term: the people value that peoples_regions[].people, names[].peoples and native[].people take for it. draft-v2.1 applies the table and flags any term not in it; verify-v2.1 checks against it and refuses an unlisted term; the validator rejects a people value outside the set of `people` values below. `pilot` says how the ten pilot entries' existing flags would change under this table; the pilot entries are not re-run or edited.

rows.term: Russian, Russians, Russian peasants, Russia, Russia's, русскій, русская, русское, русскіе, русскія, русскаго, русской, русскому, русскомъ, русскую, русскою, русскихъ, русскимъ, русскими, Россіи, Россіей, Россійской, Россійскомъ, россіяне
rows.reasoning: The sources name the people directly. Where a page says only "the peasants" inside a passage about Russia (Ralston's Russian peasants), the context fixes Russians, as draft-v2 already ruled.
rows.note: The context rule is the narrowest reading; it is not used to file a named Little-Russian or White-Russian region as Russian. "Russia" and "Россіи" can name the whole Empire, which took in Little-Russia and White-Russia, and Afanasyev's "русскій" sometimes covers all the East Slavs: a row rests on these forms only where the passage names no other people, and the entry's region keeps the source's word.
rows.pilot: No change. Rows filed this way in all ten pilot entries stand.

rows.reasoning: Ralston writes "In the Government of Archangel tradition tells of Twelve Midnight Sisters" (1872 p.148), from Afanasyev's "въ архангельской губер. знаютъ двѣнадцать сестеръ полуночницъ" (1869 p.77). Archangel was a Great Russian government.
rows.note: Only the government forms are listed: "Archangel" alone also means the archangel.
rows.pilot: No pilot entry uses the term; nothing changes.

rows.reasoning: "No woman in the Olonets Government thinks of laying aside her spindle without uttering a prayer" (Ralston 1872 p.133), from Afanasyev's "въ олонецкой губ. ни одна баба не покидаетъ ..." (1868 p.101). Olonets was a Great Russian government.
rows.note: The government also held Karelians and Vepsians, who are not Slavs and get no row; the pages speak of the Russian peasant women there.

rows.reasoning: "In the Tomsk Government, on the Eve of the Epiphany, the peasants place ... little cakes" (Ralston 1872 p.134), and Afanasyev's "въ томской губ. сильному («жгучему») морозу дается эпитетъ" (1865 p.583). Tomsk is a Siberian government, and the table already maps Siberia to Russians.
rows.note: The government also held Siberian peoples who are not Slavs and get no row; both pages speak of Russian settlers.

rows.reasoning: Ralston's footnote to the Frost tale gives a Russian variant from Afanasyev as "written down in Kazan" (1873 p.223). The tale is in Russian, in a Russian collection, and Kazan was a government of European Russia whose largest people was the Russians.
rows.note: Kazan was also the chief city of the Tatars, who are not Slavs and get no row; the page fixes only where the tale was written down, and the table reads its teller as Russian.

rows.reasoning: Ralston writes "In a variant from the Kursk Government (Afanasief IV. No 42. b), the stepdaughter is left by her father" (1873 p.221). Most of the government was Great Russian.
rows.note: Follows the Voroneje row: the south-western districts of Kursk were largely Little-Russian (Ukrainian) settlement, and the page does not say which district the variant came from, so a reader may file it as Ukrainians.

rows.reasoning: Afanasyev writes "Поѣздъ Чумы въ Подоліи называютъ гоминъ" and tells the legend of a "Подолянинъ" who met it, whom the same passage calls a "русинъ" (1869 p.111), and "Въ подольской губ. вѣрятъ, что нечистый можетъ являться" (1865 p.529). Podolia was a government of Little-Russia; same rule as Kief and Chernigof.
rows.note: Podolia belonged to Poland until 1793 and its landowners and towns were largely Polish and Jewish, so a reader may file a Podolian usage as Poles; the pilot's context rule would have filed it as Russians. The table follows Kief and Chernigof and the page's own "русинъ".

rows.reasoning: Ralston sets "a version of the story which comes from the Bukovina" beside "the German or the Russian tale" (1873 p.286). The Slavs of the Bukovina were the Ruthenians, whom the table maps to Ukrainians; the Hutsuls row already places them there.
rows.note: The page names a place, not a people, and the Bukovina was also Romanian and German-speaking; a Romanian version would get no row, since Romanians are not Slavs. Karadžić's "буковина" (beech wood) is a common noun and is not listed.

rows.term: хорутане, хорутанъ, хорутанская, хорутанской, хорутанскому, хорутанскомъ, хорутанскимъ, хорутанскихъ, хорутанскою, хорутанскую, хорутанскія ("Carinthian")
rows.reasoning: In 19th-century Russian the хорутане are the Slovenes (of Carinthia, Carniola and Styria). Afanasyev cites "хорутанской приповѣдки" (1868 p.295), "Въ хорутанской редакціи этой сказки" (1868 p.311) and "По хорутанскому преданію, Куга переѣзжала на ладьѣ черезъ рѣку Саву" (1869 p.113), the Sava being the Slovene river.
rows.note: The word is a regional name for the Slovenes, not an umbrella; the entry's region keeps "хорутанскій" where it matters.
